def: Binary fission and budding are simple asexual reproduction methods used by lower animals, where offspring arise without gamete formation or fertilization.
points: In binary fission, the parent cell divides into two equal daughter cells, each growing into a complete organism (e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium).
The nucleus divides first by mitosis, followed by division of the cytoplasm.
In budding, a small outgrowth called a bud forms on the parent body.
The bud grows, develops organs, and may detach (Hydra) or remain attached forming a colony (sponges, corals).
Both methods produce offspring genetically identical to the parent.
These methods are fast and suited to simple-bodied organisms living in favourable, stable conditions.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Parent cell"] --> B["Binary fission: splits into 2 equal cells"]
  A --> C["Budding: outgrowth (bud) forms"]
  C --> D["Bud grows and detaches or stays attached"]

example: Hydra reproduces by budding: a bud appears on its body wall, grows tentacles and a mouth, then detaches as a new small Hydra.
tip: State the organism name with each method (Amoeba for fission, Hydra for budding) — examiners specifically check for correct examples.

def: Spermatogenesis is the formation of sperm in the testis, and oogenesis is the formation of the ovum in the ovary; both convert diploid germ cells into haploid gametes through meiosis.
points: Spermatogenesis occurs in seminiferous tubules: spermatogonium (2n) divides by mitosis then meiosis I and II to give 4 haploid spermatids.
Spermatids transform into mature sperm by spermiogenesis (losing cytoplasm, gaining a tail).
Oogenesis occurs in the ovary: oogonium (2n) grows into a primary oocyte which undergoes meiosis I to form a secondary oocyte and first polar body.
Meiosis II (completed only after fertilization) gives one functional ovum and a second polar body.
Spermatogenesis gives 4 equal functional sperm; oogenesis gives only 1 functional ovum due to unequal cytoplasm division.
Both processes are controlled by hormones: FSH and LH from the pituitary act on the testis/ovary.
formula: 1 spermatogonium -> 4 functional sperm;  1 oogonium -> 1 functional ovum + polar bodies

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Spermatogonium 2n"] --> B["Primary spermatocyte"]
  B --> C["Secondary spermatocytes (meiosis I)"]
  C --> D["4 Spermatids (meiosis II)"]
  D --> E["4 mature sperm"]

example: In humans, spermatogenesis takes about 65-75 days, continuously from puberty, while oogenesis begins before birth but each egg completes its final division only when fertilized.
tip: Draw two separate simple flow diagrams side by side and highlight the key difference: equal 4 sperm vs only 1 functional ovum.

def: The menstrual cycle is the roughly 28-day hormonal cycle in human females that prepares the uterus for possible pregnancy, divided into menstrual, follicular, ovulatory and luteal phases.
points: Menstrual phase (day 1-5): shedding of the endometrium, if no fertilization occurred in the previous cycle.
Follicular phase: FSH stimulates growth of ovarian follicles, which secrete estrogen causing endometrium to thicken.
Ovulatory phase: a sharp surge in LH around day 14 triggers rupture of the Graafian follicle, releasing the ovum (ovulation).
Luteal phase: the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, secreting progesterone to maintain the endometrium.
If fertilization does not occur, corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and menstruation starts again.
If fertilization occurs, the developing embryo maintains the corpus luteum through hCG, and the cycle stops (pregnancy).

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Menstrual phase"] --> B["Follicular phase (FSH, estrogen)"]
  B --> C["Ovulation (LH surge)"]
  C --> D["Luteal phase (progesterone)"]
  D --> A

example: If ovulation happens on day 14 and fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum breaks down by around day 26, and menstruation begins again near day 28.
tip: Draw the cycle as a circular flow with hormone names at each stage — this diagram alone can fetch 2 marks.

def: Fertilization is the fusion of sperm and ovum to form a zygote, and implantation is the attachment of the resulting blastocyst to the uterine wall.
points: Fertilization usually occurs in the ampullary region of the fallopian tube.
A sperm penetrates the zona pellucida of the ovum and the two nuclei fuse to form a diploid zygote.
The zygote divides repeatedly (cleavage) while moving towards the uterus, forming a morula and then a blastocyst.
The blastocyst has an outer trophoblast layer and an inner cell mass that will form the embryo.
The trophoblast attaches to and digests into the endometrium; this attachment is called implantation.
After implantation, the trophoblast develops into the placenta, which connects the embryo to the mother.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Sperm + Ovum"] --> B["Zygote"]
  B --> C["Cleavage: Morula"]
  C --> D["Blastocyst"]
  D --> E["Implantation in endometrium"]

example: Implantation normally happens about 6-7 days after fertilization, once the blastocyst has travelled down the fallopian tube into the uterus.
tip: Mention the location of fertilization (ampulla of fallopian tube) specifically — a common fill-in-the-blank point.

def: Pregnancy (gestation) is the period during which the embryo develops inside the uterus, and parturition is the process of childbirth at the end of this period.
points: The placenta formed after implantation supplies nutrients and oxygen to the fetus and removes waste, also secreting hormones like hCG, estrogen and progesterone.
High progesterone during pregnancy keeps the uterus relaxed and prevents early contractions.
Human gestation lasts about 9 months (280 days from the last menstrual period).
Near full term, signals from the fully grown fetus and placenta trigger mild uterine contractions, known as the Ferguson reflex.
The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin, which causes strong uterine contractions leading to parturition (birth).
After birth, the placenta is also expelled as the afterbirth.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Full-term fetus signals"] --> B["Mild uterine contractions"]
  B --> C["Oxytocin released"]
  C --> D["Strong contractions"]
  D --> E["Parturition (birth)"]

example: Human gestation period is about 9 months (around 280 days); oxytocin injections are sometimes used medically to induce labour when parturition is delayed.
tip: Name both key hormones (progesterone for maintaining pregnancy, oxytocin for triggering birth) — a frequent 1-mark question.

def: Lactation is the production and release of milk from the mammary glands of a mother after childbirth, controlled by hormones.
points: During pregnancy, estrogen and progesterone stimulate growth and development of mammary gland tissue.
After childbirth, the hormone prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates milk production (synthesis) in the mammary glands.
The suckling action of the baby stimulates release of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary.
Oxytocin causes contraction of muscle cells around the milk glands, pushing milk out (milk ejection reflex).
The first milk secreted, called colostrum, is rich in antibodies (especially IgA) that protect the newborn.
Continued suckling maintains prolactin and oxytocin release, keeping up milk supply.
formula: Prolactin -> milk synthesis;  Oxytocin -> milk ejection

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Baby suckles"] --> B["Prolactin: milk made"]
  A --> C["Oxytocin: milk ejected"]
  B --> D["Milk stored in gland"]
  C --> D

example: Colostrum, the yellowish first milk produced in the initial days after birth, gives the newborn passive immunity through maternal antibodies.
tip: Clearly separate the role of prolactin (making milk) from oxytocin (releasing milk) — this distinction is often tested directly.
